description: CHS Ring Zero is three students from Catholic High School, Sibu (Junior). We are building A1-37 VIGIL, a crew health monitor that catches the slow health changes astronauts cannot see in themselves. Wallance: systems programming. Kayla: web and data visualisation. Nathania: hardware and sensors. Our school animal is the penguin, and emperor penguins keep a two-month vigil, as VIGIL does for a crew.
summary: A1-37 VIGIL is a fault-tolerant crew-health monitor that runs on a bare-metal operating system kernel we wrote ourselves. It tracks five simulated vital signs and compares each astronaut against their own baseline, showing a colour-coded GREEN, AMBER or RED status with a short advice line and a "ground attention" alert. A keyboard-only astronaut console on the same kernel adds a health guide that explains each indicator and the spaceflight hazards behind it, a check-in for blood sugar and mood typed in by the astronaut, and three mini-tests (reaction, memory, mental math) that are tracked against the astronaut's own baseline. A browser Ground Station shows charts and alerts for the ground team. This addresses the challenge by helping astronauts assess and act on their own health on long missions. It matters because space radiation can flip bits in memory and silently corrupt a reading: VIGIL stores each value in three copies with a majority vote, and corrected all 100 faults injected in five 20-fault runs. Vital signs are simulated, and VIGIL is fault-tolerant, not radiation-proof.
details:
A1-37 VIGIL is a fault-tolerant crew-health monitor that runs on a bare-metal operating system kernel we wrote ourselves (i686, booted with GRUB, tested in QEMU). It answers the challenge "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions".

WHAT IT DOES

VIGIL watches five vital signs (heart rate, SpO2, body temperature, blood pressure, sleep hours) and compares each person with their OWN baseline, not a population average. If a sustained drift appears, it shows GREEN, AMBER or RED with a short advice line (for example "Rest, hydrate, re-measure within 24 hours" or "Contact the flight surgeon"). The thresholds are demo values, not clinical values.

ASTRONAUT CONSOLE (keyboard only, on the kernel)

- A health guide with 8 pages (heart rate, SpO2, blood pressure, temperature, sleep, blood sugar, mood, cognitive check). Each page explains what it is, why it is checked, how spaceflight hazards affect it, when to alert the crew or flight surgeon, and a safe general action.

- A check-in for blood sugar (mg/dL) and mood (1-5), entered by the astronaut.

- Three mini-tests: reaction time, memory and mental math, measured from the person using the keyboard.

- Each result is compared with the astronaut's own baseline and shown in colour. A "GROUND ATTENTION" line tells the astronaut what to do, and the results are sent to the ground team over the telemetry link.

A browser Ground Station shows live charts, colour status and the same alert for the ground team.

WHY OUR OWN KERNEL

Space radiation is one of NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight, and it can flip bits in memory. A monitor that silently shows a wrong value is dangerous. Every stored value (the vital baselines, and the check-in and test results) is kept in three copies with a majority vote (software triple modular redundancy) and scrubbed every second. In five separate 20-fault runs, all 20 injected bit flips were corrected each time (100 of 100). Repair time depends on where an injection lands in the 1-second scrub cycle: it ranged from about 50 to 980 ms across the runs. The raw logs are in the repository. In the 8-week simulated replay, the rule raised AMBER on day 47.

HONESTY NOTES

All five vital signs and the 8-week replay are SIMULATED and labelled so on screen and in the video. Blood sugar and mood are typed in by the astronaut, and test results are measured from the person using the keyboard (10 ms timing resolution under QEMU). History is lost on reboot. VIGIL is fault-tolerant, not radiation-proof. We did not test with real radiation or on a person.

NOT COVERED YET

Camera or image input, focus and coordination tests, a clickable body figure, real sensors, and saving history across reboots.

HOW WE BUILT IT

C and assembly for the kernel (framebuffer screen, PS/2 keyboard, serial port, 100 Hz timer), Python for the bridge that simulates vitals and relays telemetry, and HTML/JavaScript with Chart.js (bundled, MIT licence) for the Ground Station.

LINKS

Code: https://github.com/WallanceWong/ringzero-kernel

TEAM

Team CHS Ring Zero, Catholic High School Sibu. Wallance Wong (kernel, bridge, fault tolerance), Kayla Wee (Ground Station dashboard design), Nathania Chua (proofreading and filming).

AI USE

AI assistance was used for ideation, coding and debugging, the README and submission text, the video edit (watermarked) and the tone audio. The kernel design and the fault-injection tests are the team's own work.
